lesson.menu_title: Midpoint Checkpoint — Measured Progress, Not Felt Progress
lesson.menu_desc: What the numbers say has changed since Lesson 1, what has not, and the one thing to train next -- 38 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 12 -- Midpoint Checkpoint
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Fernando Meneghelli Bottura | Lesson 12 -- Midpoint Checkpoint

listenings.text: The thing I have to explain to almost every adult learner at some point is that the feeling of progress and the fact of progress are two different measurements, and they do not move together. What happens is this. In the first months you improve and you feel it, because the things you fix are visible. Then you get past the obvious problems and the improvement continues, but it becomes invisible to you, because what is improving now is speed of retrieval, or recovery after a mistake, and nobody experiences those from the inside. Meanwhile your standard rises. Every week you notice things you would not have noticed a month ago, so you feel worse while performing better. This is the point where people conclude they have plateaued and stop, and they are almost always wrong. The answer is not to try harder. It is to measure something specific and compare it with a baseline, because feeling is a terrible instrument and a stopwatch is a very good one.

Deliberate practice is a phrase people use loosely, so let me be precise about what it actually means, because it is not the same as practising more. It means isolating the part you are worst at and repeating only that, under conditions slightly harder than the real thing, with feedback that arrives immediately. A pianist does not play the whole piece again. They play the four bars that break, forty times, slowly, then at speed. For somebody preparing for interviews in a second language, the equivalent is not having more conversations. It is taking the four seconds after a hard question, and doing only those four seconds, twenty times, with somebody who tells you at once what happened. It is boring, it is uncomfortable, and it is roughly ten times more efficient than a pleasant hour of general conversation.

extra_audio.text: Diane asks Fernando what he thinks has changed since the first lesson. Fernando says he feels roughly the same as before. Diane reads him the numbers from the baseline recording. Fernando notices that the measurement disagrees with the feeling. Diane names the one thing to train for the second half of the programme.

reading.rtitle: Why the feeling of progress is the worst instrument you own
paras: There is a point in every long piece of learning where the person doing it concludes that they have stopped improving. It arrives reliably, somewhere near the middle, and it is almost always false. The mechanism is worth understanding, because knowing it is the difference between finishing and stopping.

Early on, improvement is visible. The problems being fixed are obvious ones, and fixing them feels like progress because it is progress you can see. Later, what improves is different in kind: speed of retrieval, recovery after a mistake, the ability to keep going when a sentence breaks. None of these are experienced from the inside. They only exist in the eyes of a listener, or in a stopwatch.

At the same time, the standard rises. Every week the learner notices errors they would not have noticed a month earlier. Perceived competence therefore falls exactly while real competence is rising, and the two lines cross somewhere around the middle. That crossing point feels like failure and is in fact the ordinary shape of the curve.

The remedy is not effort. It is measurement. Record something at the beginning, record the same thing at the midpoint, and compare them with a number rather than an impression: seconds to the first word, number of recoveries, answers that opened with a conclusion. Feeling is a terrible instrument. A stopwatch is a very good one, and it does not have a bad week.
reading.source: Adapted from research on adult language learning

gist.prompt: What is the main point of this text?
choices: Most learners genuinely stop improving around the middle of a long programme.
Perceived progress falls while real progress rises, so measurement has to replace feeling.
The solution to a plateau is to increase the number of hours of study.
